skyr.name: Skyr
skyr.summary: A traditional Icelandic cultured dairy product resembling strained yogurt, part of Icelandic cuisine for centuries.

church-frescos-in-denmark.name: Kalkmalerier
church-frescos-in-denmark.summary: Danish church wall paintings found in about 600 churches, mostly dating to the Middle Ages, uncovered during 19th-century restorations after being hidden under limewash.

gotland.name: Gotland
gotland.summary: Sweden's largest island and a province in the Baltic Sea, home to about 61,000 people, most in its main town, Visby.

majestatis.name: Majestatis
majestatis.summary: Romanesque stone sculptor active in the second half of the 12th century, known for richly decorated baptismal fonts in Scania and on Gotland.

byzantios.name: Byzantios
byzantios.summary: A modern label for a Romanesque stone sculptor or workshop active on Gotland in the late 12th century, known for a group of similar baptismal fonts showing Byzantine influence.

runestone.name: Runestone
runestone.summary: A raised stone bearing a runic memorial inscription, a tradition from the 4th to 12th centuries found mostly in Scandinavia, especially Sweden, with most survivors from the late Viking Age.

elmelunde-master.name: Elmelunde Master
elmelunde-master.summary: Anonymous name given to a 16th-century Danish artist who painted distinctive frescoes, rediscovered under whitewash, in three churches on the island of Møn.

biblia-pauperum.name: Biblia pauperum
biblia-pauperum.summary: A medieval 'Paupers' Bible,' a tradition of picture Bibles, often printed as block-books, placing illustrations at the centre to show correspondences between Old and New Testament stories.

viklau-madonna.name: Viklau Madonna
viklau-madonna.summary: A late 12th-century wooden statuette of Mary, likely made on Gotland, one of Europe's best-preserved wooden sculptures from that century; a hidden relic was found inside it in 2017.

olaf-tryggvason.name: Olaf Tryggvason
olaf-tryggvason.summary: King of Norway from 995 to 1000 who forcibly promoted Christianity, is said to have founded Trondheim in 997, and died in 1000.

battle-of-svolder.name: Battle of Svolder
battle-of-svolder.summary: A naval battle fought in September 1000 in the western Baltic Sea, in which King Olaf of Norway was defeated by an alliance of the kings of Denmark and Sweden and his Norwegian enemies, tied to Norway's unification and Christianization.

magnus-erlingsson.name: Magnus Erlingsson
magnus-erlingsson.summary: King of Norway, also called Magnus V, during the civil war era, who helped establish primogeniture in royal succession and was killed at the Battle of Fimreite in 1184.

erling-skakke.name: Erling Skakke
erling-skakke.summary: Norwegian jarl (1115–1179) and father of Magnus Erlingsson, who reigned as King of Norway from 1161 to 1184.

battle-of-fimreite.name: Battle of Fimreite
battle-of-fimreite.summary: A naval battle on 15 June 1184 in which Sverre Sigurdsson's forces defeated and killed King Magnus Erlingsson, letting Sverre seize the Norwegian throne, which he held until 1202.

sverre-of-norway.name: Sverre Sigurdsson
sverre-of-norway.summary: King of Norway from 1184 to 1202, considered one of the most important rulers in Norwegian history, who rose to power leading the rebel Birkebeiner faction and was later excommunicated after conflict with the Church.

swein-forkbeard.name: Sweyn Forkbeard
swein-forkbeard.summary: King of Denmark from about 986 and briefly King of England from December 1013 until his death in 1014, and father of King Cnut.

olof-sk-tkonung.name: Olof Skötkonung
olof-sk-tkonung.summary: King of Sweden from around 995 to 1022, the first to rule both Swedes and Geats, mint coins, and become a Christian ruler in central Sweden.

eir-kr-h-konarson.name: Eirik Hákonarson
eir-kr-h-konarson.summary: Earl of Lade, Governor of Norway and Earl of Northumbria (960s–1020s) who fought at the Battle of Hjörungavágr and the Battle of Svolder, and helped conquer England for King Cnut.

jomsvikings.name: Jomsvikings
jomsvikings.summary: Legendary order of Viking mercenaries from the 10th and 11th centuries, said to worship the Old Norse gods yet fight for any lord who paid, known mainly from Icelandic sagas.

gunnar-h-mundarson.name: Gunnar of Hlíðarendi
gunnar-h-mundarson.summary: A 10th-century Icelandic chieftain, also called Gunnar of Hlíðarendi, who features prominently in the first half of Njáls saga, which recounts events leading to his death in battle.

nj-ll-orgeirsson.name: Njáll Þorgeirsson
nj-ll-orgeirsson.summary: A 10th- and early-11th-century Icelandic lawyer and one of the main figures in Njáls saga, killed when his home at Bergþórshvoll was burned.

berg-ra-skarph-insd-ttir.name: Bergþóra Skarphéðinsdóttir
berg-ra-skarph-insd-ttir.summary: A 10th-century Icelandic woman who appears in Njáls saga as an inciter of its central feud.

k-ri-s-lmundarson.name: Kári Sölmundarson
k-ri-s-lmundarson.summary: A Hebridean viking and soldier of fortune who lived in the late tenth and early eleventh centuries, a major character in Njál's Saga and grandson of an Icelander exiled for murder before the Althing was established.

nj-ls-saga.name: Njáls saga
nj-ls-saga.summary: A 13th-century Icelandic saga describing events between 960 and 1020, centered on the blood feuds surrounding the lawyer Njáll Þorgeirsson and the warrior Gunnar Hámundarson.

sigurd-the-crusader.name: Sigurd the Crusader
sigurd-the-crusader.summary: King of Norway from 1103 to 1130, known as the Crusader King as one of three co-regents who took part in the Norwegian Crusade of 1107–1110, regarded as the first king to take part in a crusade.

sm-land.name: Småland
sm-land.summary: A historical province in southern Sweden whose name means 'small lands', referring to the many small provinces that once made it up.

adam-of-bremen.name: Adam of Bremen
adam-of-bremen.summary: German medieval chronicler (before 1050 – 1081/1085) known for his history of the Hamburg church, and the first European to write about the New World, mentioning the Norse outpost of Vinland.

resund.name: Øresund
resund.summary: A strait separating Denmark from Sweden that links the Baltic Sea to the Atlantic Ocean, one of the world's busiest waterways.

earls-of-lade.name: Jarls of Lade
earls-of-lade.summary: A dynasty of Norse jarls who ruled Trøndelag and Hålogaland, in what is now Norway, from the 9th to the 11th century, seated near Trondheim.

battle-of-nesjar.name: Battle of Nesjar
battle-of-nesjar.summary: A 1016 sea battle off Norway's coast, a key event in King Olav Haraldsson's reign, later commemorated by the poem Nesjavísur and a monument at Helgeroa.

battle-of-stiklestad.name: Battle of Stiklestad
battle-of-stiklestad.summary: A 1030 battle, one of the most famous in Norwegian history, in which King Olaf II of Norway was killed; he was later declared a saint in 1164.

magnus-the-good.name: Magnus the Good
magnus-the-good.summary: Illegitimate son of Saint Olaf who became King of Norway in 1035 and King of Denmark in 1042, ruling both until his death in 1047 under unclear circumstances.

sturlunga-saga.name: Sturlunga saga
sturlunga-saga.summary: A collection of Icelandic sagas compiled around 1300, covering Iceland's history between 1117 and 1264, centered on the Sturlungs family.

gissur-orvaldsson.name: Gissur Þorvaldsson
gissur-orvaldsson.summary: A 13th-century Icelandic chieftain (1208–1268) who fought in the Age of the Sturlungs civil war, led the killing of saga-writer Snorri Sturluson in 1241 on the order of the King of Norway, and later became Earl of Iceland.

lee-m-hollander.name: Lee M. Hollander
lee-m-hollander.summary: An American philologist (1880–1972) who specialized in Old Norse studies and led the Germanic Languages department at the University of Texas at Austin.

einar-thambarskelfir.name: Einar Thambarskelfir
einar-thambarskelfir.summary: An influential Norwegian noble and politician (c. 980–c. 1050) who led feudal lords against King Olaf Haraldsson and appears in Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla.

heimskringla.name: Heimskringla
heimskringla.summary: The best-known collection of Old Norwegian kings' sagas, written in Old Norse in Iceland and likely composed by Snorri Sturluson around 1230.

prose-edda.name: Prose Edda
prose-edda.summary: An early 13th-century Old Norse textbook from Iceland, largely compiled by Snorri Sturluson, considered the fullest source for modern knowledge of Norse mythology.

snorri-sturluson.name: Snorri Sturluson
snorri-sturluson.summary: An Icelandic historian, poet and politician (1179–1241) credited with the Prose Edda and Heimskringla, key sources on Norse mythology and kings; he was assassinated in 1241.

poetic-edda.name: Poetic Edda
poetic-edda.summary: A collection of anonymous Old Norse poems in alliterative verse, based on the medieval Icelandic Codex Regius manuscript, central to the study of Norse mythology.

christianization-of-scandinavia.name: Christianization of Scandinavia
christianization-of-scandinavia.summary: The gradual conversion of Denmark, Norway and Sweden to Christianity between the 9th and 12th centuries, driven largely by kings who saw the new religion as politically advantageous.

medieval-runes.name: Medieval runes
medieval-runes.summary: A Scandinavian runic alphabet that evolved from the Younger Futhark, fully formed by the early 13th century and used throughout Scandinavia into the 16th century.

skald.name: Skald
skald.summary: A poet who composed skaldic poetry, an ornate form of Old Norse verse using kennings, often to honor Viking-era kings.

gylfaginning.name: Gylfaginning
gylfaginning.summary: The first main part of the 13th-century Prose Edda, a dialogue describing the creation and eventual destruction of the world in Norse mythology.

sk-ldskaparm-l.name: Skáldskaparmál
sk-ldskaparm-l.summary: The second part of Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda, mixing Norse mythology with a poetic thesaurus of kennings intended for skalds.

h-ttatal.name: Háttatal
h-ttatal.summary: Final section of Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda, a roughly 20,000-word showcase of Old Norse verse forms that both describes and prescribes poetic rules.

gunnlaugr-leifsson.name: Gunnlaugr Leifsson
gunnlaugr-leifsson.summary: An Icelandic scholar, author and poet, and a Benedictine monk at the Þingeyraklaustur monastery, often called Gunnlaugr the Monk; he died in 1218 or 1219.

merl-n-ssp.name: Merlínússpá
merl-n-ssp.summary: An Old Norse-Icelandic verse translation, made around 1200 by Gunnlaugr Leifsson, of a Latin prophecy from Geoffrey of Monmouth's history of Britain; the earliest Arthurian text translated in medieval Scandinavia.

geoffrey-of-monmouth.name: Geoffrey of Monmouth
geoffrey-of-monmouth.summary: A Christian cleric from Wales (c. 1095–c. 1155) whose chronicle, the History of the Kings of Britain, popularised tales of King Arthur though later judged historically unreliable.

prophetiae-merlini.name: Prophetiae Merlini
prophetiae-merlini.summary: A Latin work by Geoffrey of Monmouth, circulated from about 1130 to 1135, containing prophecies attributed to the legendary wizard Merlin, later folded into his larger Historia Regum Britanniae.

mead-of-poetry.name: Mead of poetry
mead-of-poetry.summary: A mythical drink in Norse mythology that lets whoever drinks it become a skilled poet or scholar able to answer any question; the myth was recorded by Snorri Sturluson and linked to the god Odin.

odin.name: Odin
odin.summary: A widely revered god of Norse mythology and Germanic paganism, associated with wisdom, poetry and frenzy, worshipped from Roman-era Germania through the Viking Age.

asgard.name: Asgard
asgard.summary: In Norse mythology, the fortified home of the Aesir gods described in the Eddas and other Old Norse texts, roughly equivalent to Mount Olympus in Greek myth.

codex-regius.name: Codex Regius
codex-regius.summary: An Icelandic manuscript from the 1270s that is the main source for most poems of the Poetic Edda, later sent to Denmark and returned to Iceland in 1971.

brynj-lfur-sveinsson.name: Brynjólfur Sveinsson
brynj-lfur-sveinsson.summary: Lutheran Bishop of Skálholt in Iceland (1605-1675) who named the collection of Old Norse poems the Edda in 1643 and worked to collect old Icelandic manuscripts.

christian-iv-of-denmark.name: Christian IV of Denmark
christian-iv-of-denmark.summary: King of Denmark and Norway from 1588 to 1648, Scandinavia's longest-reigning monarch, remembered for ambitious reforms and for leading Denmark–Norway into the costly Thirty Years' War.

royal-danish-library.name: Royal Danish Library
royal-danish-library.summary: Denmark's national library, formed in 2017 by merging the State and University Library in Aarhus with the former Royal Library in Copenhagen, still maintaining both locations.

egil-s-saga.name: Egil's Saga
egil-s-saga.summary: Icelandic family saga tracing the life of Egill Skallagrímsson and his kin from about 850 to 1000, likely written by Snorri Sturluson.

egill-skallagr-msson.name: Egill Skallagrímsson
egill-skallagr-msson.summary: Viking Age war poet, sorcerer and farmer (c. 904–995), the anti-hero of Egil's Saga.

s-mundr-fr-i.name: Sæmundr the Learned
s-mundr-fr-i.summary: An Icelandic priest and scholar known as Sæmundr the Learned, who lived from 1056 to 1133.

v-lusp.name: Völuspá
v-lusp.summary: The best-known poem of the Poetic Edda, dating to the tenth century, describing the creation, end and rebirth of the world in Norse mythology.

v-lusp-hin-skamma.name: Völuspá hin skamma
v-lusp-hin-skamma.summary: An Old Norse poem, 'The Short Völuspá', surviving only in a few stanzas within other texts and dated to around the twelfth century.

trajan.name: Trajan
trajan.summary: Roman emperor from 98 to 117 CE, one of the Five Good Emperors, whose conquests brought the empire to its greatest territorial extent; born in what is now southern Spain.

dacia-scandinavia.name: Scandinavian Dacia
dacia-scandinavia.summary: A name for Denmark (and sometimes all Scandinavia) used through the Middle Ages, coined by 11th-century historian Dudo of Saint-Quentin's false etymology linking Danes to the ancient Dacians.

dacia.name: Dacia
dacia.summary: The historical region in and around modern Romania inhabited by the Dacians, united under King Burebista from 82 BC until the Roman conquest in AD 106.

oddr-snorrason.name: Oddr Snorrason
oddr-snorrason.summary: 12th-century Icelandic Benedictine monk at Þingeyraklaustur, Iceland's first monastery, founded in 1133.

l-fs-saga-tryggvasonar.name: Óláfs saga Tryggvasonar
l-fs-saga-tryggvasonar.summary: A name for several medieval kings' sagas about the life of the 10th-century Norwegian king Óláfr Tryggvason, thought to be based on now-lost Latin biographies.

l-fs-saga-tryggvasonar-en-mesta.name: Óláfs saga Tryggvasonar en mesta
l-fs-saga-tryggvasonar-en-mesta.summary: The longest and latest (c. 1300) saga about King Óláfr Tryggvason, compiled from earlier biographies and other sources, covering his conversion to Christianity in detail.

younger-futhark.name: Younger Futhark
younger-futhark.summary: A 16-character runic alphabet in use from around the 9th century, a reduced form of the older Elder Futhark used through the Viking Age.

bryggen-inscriptions.name: Bryggen inscriptions
bryggen-inscriptions.summary: Around 670 medieval runic inscriptions on wood and bone found since 1955 in Bergen, Norway, showing runes were still used for everyday messages as late as the 14th century.

cnut.name: Cnut
cnut.summary: King of England from 1016, Denmark from 1018, and Norway from 1028 until his death in 1035, ruling the three kingdoms together as the North Sea Empire.

north-sea-empire.name: North Sea Empire
north-sea-empire.summary: Personal union of England, Denmark and Norway under Norse kings for most of 1013 to 1042; at its height under Cnut the Great it was the most powerful realm in western Europe after the Holy Roman Empire.

nidaros.name: Nidaros
nidaros.summary: Medieval name for Trondheim, capital of Norway's first Christian kings and home to the shrine of Saint Olaf, a major pilgrimage site.

uppsala.name: Uppsala
uppsala.summary: Sweden's fourth-largest city, the ecclesiastical centre of the country since 1164, and seat of Scandinavia's oldest university, founded in 1477.

canute-iv-of-denmark.name: Canute IV
canute-iv-of-denmark.summary: King of Denmark from 1080 to 1086, slain by rebels in 1086 and the first Danish king to be canonized; the Catholic Church later recognized him as Denmark's patron saint in 1101.

housecarl.name: Housecarl
housecarl.summary: A well-trained, salaried household bodyguard used in medieval Scandinavia and, from the 11th century, Anglo-Saxon England, including at the Battle of Hastings.

st-canute-s-cathedral.name: Odense Cathedral
st-canute-s-cathedral.summary: A cathedral in Odense, Denmark, named for King Canute the Saint, whose remains, along with his brother's, are displayed in its crypt.

harthacnut.name: Harthacnut
harthacnut.summary: King of Denmark from 1035 and King of England from 1040 until his death in 1042, son of Cnut the Great, and the last Dane to rule England.

sweyn-ii-of-denmark.name: Sweyn Estridsson
sweyn-ii-of-denmark.summary: King of Denmark from 1047 to 1076, grandson of Sweyn Forkbeard, described as courageous in battle though not very successful as a military commander.

pope-adrian-iv.name: Nicholas Breakspear (Pope Adrian IV)
pope-adrian-iv.summary: An Englishman from Hertfordshire who became Pope Adrian IV, head of the Catholic Church from 1154 to 1159, the only pope born in England.

tovi-the-proud.name: Tovi the Proud
tovi-the-proud.summary: Rich and powerful 11th-century Danish thegn holding estates across southern England, who served as staller (a court official) to King Cnut the Great.

anglo-saxon-chronicle.name: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
anglo-saxon-chronicle.summary: A set of Old English annals on Anglo-Saxon history, first compiled in the late 800s under King Alfred the Great and copied and updated at English monasteries until 1154; its oldest surviving manuscript, held at Cambridge, is called the Parker Chronicle.

h-vam-l.name: Hávamál
h-vam-l.summary: Old Norse poem attributed to Odin, dated to around 900–1000 CE, offering practical and philosophical wisdom on conduct, plus an account of how Odin won the runes.

nicomachean-ethics.name: Nicomachean Ethics
nicomachean-ethics.summary: Aristotle's best-known work on ethics, exploring how to live well and what constitutes the good; hugely influential on medieval philosophy.

gu-mundur-finnbogason.name: Guðmundur Finnbogason
gu-mundur-finnbogason.summary: Icelandic philosopher (1873–1944) and one of the first Icelandic psychologists, whose work influenced Jean Piaget's development stages model.

sveinbjorn-johnson.name: Sveinbjorn Johnson
sveinbjorn-johnson.summary: Icelandic-born American lawyer, politician and scholar (1883-1946).

homer.name: Homer
homer.summary: Ancient Greek poet, possibly born around the 8th century BC, traditionally credited as author of the Iliad and the Odyssey, foundational works of Greek literature.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

euhemerism.name: Euhemerism
euhemerism.summary: An approach to interpreting mythology as having originated from real historical events later exaggerated in the retelling, named after the Greek mythographer Euhemerus (late 4th century BC).

vedas.name: Vedas
vedas.summary: A large body of ancient Indian religious texts and the oldest layer of Sanskrit literature, orally transmitted since the 2nd millennium BCE and regarded as the oldest scriptures of Hinduism.

harald-bluetooth.name: Harald Bluetooth
harald-bluetooth.summary: King of Denmark and Norway (r. c. 958-986), son of Gorm the Old and Thyra; his own son Swein Forkbeard forced him from the throne shortly before his death.

jelling-stones.name: Jelling stones
jelling-stones.summary: Two massive 10th-century runestones at Jelling, Denmark; the older honors King Gorm the Old's wife, the larger celebrates his son Harald Bluetooth's conquests and his Christianizing of the Danes. Since 1994 part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.

anders-winroth.name: Anders Winroth
anders-winroth.summary: A Swedish medievalist, born 1965, who has taught at the University of Oslo and previously at Yale University.

dudo-of-saint-quentin.name: Dudo of Saint-Quentin
dudo-of-saint-quentin.summary: A Picard historian and dean of Saint-Quentin (born 960s, died before 1043) who, at Duke Richard I's request, wrote a history of the Normans' customs and origins.

dacians.name: Dacians
dacians.summary: The ancient Indo-European-speaking people of Dacia, near the Carpathians and west of the Black Sea, closely related to the Getae and often grouped with the Thracians.

dominican-order.name: Dominican Order
dominican-order.summary: Catholic mendicant order, also called the Order of Preachers, founded in France by Dominic de Guzmán and approved by Pope Honorius III in 1216; known for its intellectual tradition.

order-of-friars-minor.name: Franciscans
order-of-friars-minor.summary: Mendicant Catholic religious order founded by Francis of Assisi in 1209, whose members preached and lived in poverty; it remains the largest of today's Franciscan orders.

carmelites.name: Carmelites
carmelites.summary: A Catholic mendicant religious order for men and women, probably founded in the 12th century on Mount Carmel in the Holy Land.

karelia.name: Karelia
karelia.summary: A cultural region of Northern Europe divided between northwestern Russia and Finland, historically significant to Russia, Finland and Sweden.

temple-at-uppsala.name: Uppsala
temple-at-uppsala.summary: The site in Sweden of a Norse pagan religious centre, described by medieval writers as holding idols near a sacred tree and well, later replaced by Christianity.

borr.name: Borr
borr.summary: In Norse mythology, the son of Búri and father of Odin, Vili and Vé, mentioned in the Poetic Edda and the Prose Edda.

thorgeir-ljosvetningagodi.name: Thorgeir Ljósvetningagoði
thorgeir-ljosvetningagodi.summary: An Icelandic lawspeaker and pagan chieftain who in 999 or 1000 decided that Iceland should adopt Christianity, averting civil conflict between pagans and Christians.

gamla-uppsala.name: Gamla Uppsala
gamla-uppsala.summary: A village near Uppsala, Sweden, that was a major religious and political center from the 3rd century CE, seat of the legendary Yngling kings and site of the assembly of all Swedes.

d-sabl-t.name: Dísablót
d-sabl-t.summary: A pre-Christian Scandinavian sacrificial festival honoring female spirits called dísir, meant to bless the harvest, usually performed by women though kings sometimes led it as high priests.

seeress-germanic.name: Völva
seeress-germanic.summary: A woman in Germanic paganism believed able to foretell the future and perform sorcery, called völva in Norse mythology, at times leading armed resistance or serving as an envoy to Rome.

sei-r.name: Seiðr
sei-r.summary: A type of Norse magic tied to foretelling and shaping the future, practiced by both women and men and associated with the god Odin and the goddess Freyja.

skara.name: Skara
skara.summary: A small Swedish town, one of the country's oldest cities, with a long educational and ecclesiastical history.

uppland.name: Uppland
uppland.summary: A historical Swedish province north of Stockholm, famous for the highest concentration of runestones in the world and home to Sweden's oldest town and university.

pope-honorius-iii.name: Cardinal Cencius (Pope Honorius III)
pope-honorius-iii.summary: Canon and Camerlengo who later became Pope Honorius III, ruling the Catholic Church and Papal States from 1216 to 1227 and promoting the Fifth Crusade.

liber-censuum.name: Liber Censuum
liber-censuum.summary: An eighteen-volume financial record of papal real estate revenues from 492 to 1192, considered one of the most valuable sources for medieval papal economics.
